lines.text: March 6th, 1940. A frozen forest near the Kollaa River, in eastern Finland.
lines.dir: low, close to the mic, unhurried

lines.text: A small man in a white smock lies in the snow, his cheek pressed against an old bolt-action rifle.
Somewhere across the clearing, a Soviet soldier sees him first.
The bullet hits his lower jaw.
His comrades drag him back unconscious. One of them later says half his face was gone.
By then, he'd been on this front for about ninety-eight days.
In that time, depending on who's counting, he'd killed more than five hundred men.
With no telescopic sight. Just the iron sights on his rifle, and a lot of patience.
His name was Simo Häyhä.
So how does a farmer with an old rifle end up with the highest sniper count of any war? And is that number even real?
Simo was born in 1905 in Rautjärvi, a farming parish a few miles from the Russian border.
He stood about five foot three. He farmed, he hunted, and he didn't talk much.
At seventeen he joined the Civil Guard, Finland's volunteer militia, and started winning shooting competitions.
At paper targets, mostly. That changed in the winter of 1939.
On November 30th, the Soviet Union invades Finland.
No declaration of war. Bombs on Helsinki on day one.
The math looks hopeless. Finland has under four million people. The Soviet Union has around one hundred seventy million.
Moscow plans for a short war. There's a story, maybe too good to be true, that some Red Army units were warned not to march into Sweden by mistake.
Simo's company, part of Infantry Regiment 34, is sent to the Kollaa River, north of Lake Ladoga.
Their orders are simple. Hold the road.
Finnish soldiers will sum up the next three months in two words. "Kollaa holds."
The Red Army has tanks, artillery and planes. What it doesn't have, out here, is roads.
Its columns crawl along narrow forest tracks, miles long, with snow up to a man's waist on either side.
Finnish troops on skis come out of the trees, cut a column into pieces, and leave each piece to freeze.
The Finns call those pockets motti. It's their word for a neat stack of firewood.
Now picture yourself on the other side of that clearing.
You're a Red Army conscript, maybe from somewhere far to the south, and it's forty degrees below zero.
Daylight lasts about six hours. The trees are white, the ground is white, and every so often someone near you just drops.
You never hear where it came from.
Here's the thing. A scope would have helped him see. It also would have helped the enemy see him.
The glass can catch the low winter sun and flash. And in that cold it can fog up or frost over.
A scope also makes you lift your head a few inches higher. Out there, a few inches is a lot.
He knew about that flash because he spent his days looking for it on the other side.
So he used a Finnish copy of a Russian rifle, the old Mosin-Nagant, and pointed it back at the Red Army.
He had other tricks.
He packed snow in front of his position and soaked it until it froze hard. That way the muzzle blast wouldn't kick up a puff of powder.
He kept snow in his mouth, so his breath wouldn't steam in the cold air.
And he lay still. For hours. Some days from before dawn until after dark.
Most of us can't get through a two-hour movie without checking our phones.
His company commander was a very different kind of man. Captain Aarne Juutilainen, a former French Foreign Legionnaire, nicknamed "the Terror of Morocco".
Juutilainen worked out quickly what he had, and started sending Simo after the Soviet snipers who were picking off his men.
A quiet farmer, a loud legionnaire. It worked.
The Red Army notices. They send counter-snipers into the woods to find him.
According to Finnish accounts, most of them don't come back.
So they try artillery, shelling whole stretches of forest where he might be.
One barrage reportedly shreds the back of his coat.
He gets up, and goes back to work.
Which raises a question. Who was counting?
On February 17th, 1940, a Finnish army report credited him with two hundred nineteen confirmed rifle kills.
Later counts, including his own wartime diary, put the figure at around five hundred.
That diary only became public in 2017, fifteen years after his death.
Many books add roughly two hundred more with a submachine gun. Nobody could really verify those.
At Kollaa, "confirmed" usually meant another soldier saw a man fall. Nobody walked into that clearing to check.
So the honest answer is, we don't know the exact number.
But take the lowest figure. Two hundred nineteen, in about eleven weeks.
Lyudmila Pavlichenko, the Soviet Union's most famous sniper, was credited with three hundred nine over about a year.
Same goes for the nickname. "The White Death" is supposed to be what the Soviets called him.
It may just as well have started in Finnish newspapers. Either way, it stuck.
Which brings us back to that morning in March.
The round that hit him is usually described as an explosive bullet.
He's unconscious for about a week. He wakes up on March 13th, 1940.
The day the war ends.
Finland gives up roughly a tenth of its territory, including much of Karelia.
But it stays an independent country. And Kollaa never fell.
Around twenty-five thousand Finns died in those hundred and five days. Soviet dead start at about one hundred twenty-six thousand, and some estimates go far higher.
Simo needs years of surgery to rebuild his jaw.
Field Marshal Mannerheim promotes him from corporal straight to second lieutenant.
Then he goes home, breeds hunting dogs, and hunts moose, sometimes with the President of Finland.
Late in life, an interviewer asks how he got so good. He answers with one word." Practice."
Asked if he regretted the killing, he said he did what he was told, as well as he could.
Simo Häyhä died in 2002, at ninety-six, in a veterans' home in Hamina.
In all those years, he never seemed very interested in the number everyone kept asking him about.
The soldiers across that clearing didn't need a number. They just learned not to stand up.
